title_en: Shanghai Jiahua Enterprise Development Co., Ltd. v. Shanghai Jiahua Education Institute — dispute over shareholders' right to know

full_text_en:
Shanghai Jiahua Enterprise Development Co., Ltd. v. Shanghai Jiahua Education Training College — dispute over a sponsor's right to information

Ruling Summary

The sponsor of a private school may independently choose to establish a non-profit or for-profit private school. Where a sponsor of a for-profit private school claims to exercise the right to information, the people's court may analogically apply the relevant provisions of the Company Law.

Plaintiff: Shanghai Jiahua Enterprise Development Co., Ltd., domiciled at Changzhong Road, Haiwan Town, Fengxian District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Fang Yufen, Chairperson of the Board of Directors.

Defendant: Shanghai Jiahua Education Training College, domiciled at Wusi Highway, Fengxian District, Shanghai.
Legal Representative: Tang Xiufeng, Vice President of the College.

The plaintiff, Shanghai Jiahua Enterprise Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jiahua Company), filed a lawsuit with the Fengxian District People's Court of Shanghai against the defendant, Shanghai Jiahua Education Training College (hereinafter referred to as Jiahua College), concerning a dispute over a sponsor's right to information.

Plaintiff's Allegations: On March 25, 2010, the plaintiff invested in and established the defendant Jiahua College, holding 100% of the investment shares. In September 2012, Jiahua Company entered into the "Contract on Transfer of Assets and Start-up Funds and Joint Operation of the School" with Tang Xiufeng, Zhao Mingyou, and Wang Wenhong, reaching agreements on matters such as the establishment of the Shanghai Jiahua Motor Vehicle Driving Training Base and the transfer and exchange of investment shares. On October 15, 2012, the board of directors of Jiahua College passed the "Board Resolution," providing that Tang Xiufeng and others held 90% of the investment shares in Jiahua College and that Jiahua Company held 10% of the investment shares. Subsequently, a dispute arose between the parties due to Tang Xiufeng and others unilaterally terminating the application for the Shanghai Jiahua Motor Vehicle Driving Training Base, among other matters. Jiahua Company then filed a lawsuit with the Pudong New Area People's Court of Shanghai. The court later rendered a judgment confirming that Jiahua Company held 50% of the investment shares in Jiahua College. In mid-November 2015, Jiahua Company sent a letter to Jiahua College requesting the provision of materials such as financial reports, board resolutions, and supervisory board resolutions, but Jiahua College has not responded to date. Therefore, Jiahua Company filed the present lawsuit with the court based on the *General Principles of the Civil Law* and the provisions of the articles of association, seeking an order: 1. That Jiahua College provide for Jiahua Company's inspection and reproduction the articles of association (including amendments thereto), resolutions of the board of directors, resolutions of the supervisory board, and financial accounting reports (including but not limited to balance sheets, income statements, statements of changes in financial position, statements of financial condition, profit distribution statements, and tax returns) from the establishment of the college in April 2010 to the present; 2. That Jiahua College provide for Jiahua Company's inspection the accounting books (including the general ledger, various subsidiary ledgers, accounts receivable/payable ledgers, cash journals, bank journals, fixed asset card lists, original vouchers, and detailed records of bank statement transactions) from the establishment of the college in April 2010 to the present.

Defendant's Defense: The defendant disagreed with the plaintiff's claims. It argued that the plaintiff's claims had no legal basis. Jiahua College was a private non-enterprise unit registered and established in accordance with the *Law of the People's Republic of China on the Promotion of Privately-Run Schools* and was a non-profit social organization. It did not fall within the four types of legal persons provided for in the *General Principles of the Civil Law*. Therefore, the organization, activities, and management of Jiahua College were not governed by the *Company Law*.

Facts Found by the Fengxian District People's Court of Shanghai at First Instance:

In April 2010, the plaintiff Jiahua Company invested in and established the defendant Jiahua College, holding 100% of the investment shares. In September 2012, Jiahua Company entered into the "Contract on Transfer of Assets and Start-up Funds and Joint Operation of the School" with Tang Xiufeng, Zhao Mingyou, and Wang Wenhong, reaching agreements on matters such as the establishment of the Shanghai Jiahua Motor Vehicle Driving Training Base and the transfer and exchange of investment shares. On October 15, 2012, the board of directors of Jiahua College passed the "Board Resolution," providing that Tang Xiufeng and others held 90% of the investment shares in Jiahua College and that Jiahua Company held 10% of the investment shares. Subsequently, a dispute arose between the parties due to the termination of the application for the Shanghai Jiahua Motor Vehicle Driving Training Base, among other matters. Jiahua Company then filed a lawsuit with the Pudong New Area People's Court of Shanghai. On June 24, 2015, the Pudong New Area People's Court of Shanghai rendered Judgment No. (2015) Pu Min Er (Shang) Chu Zi No. 62, confirming that Jiahua Company held a total of 50% of the investment shares in Jiahua College. The said judgment has become legally effective. In mid-November 2015, Jiahua Company sent a letter to Jiahua College requesting the provision of materials such as financial reports, board resolutions, and supervisory board resolutions. As Jiahua College did not reply, Jiahua Company filed the present lawsuit with the court.

It was also found that the defendant Jiahua College is a legal-person-type private non-enterprise unit, with the issuing authority being the Fengxian District Civil Affairs Bureau of Shanghai and the competent business authority being the Fengxian District Education Bureau of Shanghai. On April 9, 2010, the articles of association of Jiahua College provided: "The College implements a system of responsibility by the president under the leadership of the board of directors, and the decision-making body is the board of directors, etc."

Opinion of the Fengxian District People's Court of Shanghai at First Instance:

A party has the burden of proof to support its own claims. The defendant Jiahua College is a legal-person-type private non-enterprise unit, which is not within the scope of regulation by the *Company Law*. Moreover, the articles of association of the College do not provide that sponsors have the right to inspect or reproduce board resolutions, financial accounting reports, accounting books, etc. Therefore, the claims made by the plaintiff Jiahua Company lack corresponding provisions in the articles of association and legal basis, and cannot be sustained.

Accordingly, pursuant to Article 64, Paragraph 1, of the *Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*, the Fengxian District People's Court of Shanghai rendered a judgment on March 18, 2016: rejecting all claims of the plaintiff Jiahua Company.

Jiahua Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, arguing:

1. The first-instance judgment had issues with fact-finding. It failed to find the fact that Article 17, Paragraph 1, Item 2, of the articles of association of the appellee Jiahua College, dated April 9, 2010, provided that sponsors have the right to "participate in the operation and management activities of the College." The right to information is the foundation for sponsors to participate in the operation and management activities of the College; without it, the right to participate in operation and management cannot be exercised at all.

2. The first-instance court erred in characterizing Jiahua College as "a legal-person-type private non-enterprise unit, not within the scope of regulation by the *Company Law*." Although Jiahua College is "a legal-person-type private non-enterprise unit," the first-instance court failed to provide any legal basis for holding that Jiahua Company, as a sponsor, could not exercise the right to information. The *Law of the People's Republic of China on the Promotion of Privately-Run Schools* (hereinafter the *Private Education Promotion Law*) contains no prohibitive provision preventing sponsors from exercising the right to information. As a sponsor, Jiahua Company should be entitled to the corresponding right to information. Therefore, Jiahua Company requested the appellate court to find the facts, reverse the original judgment in accordance with the law, and amend the judgment to support all claims made by Jiahua Company at first instance.

The appellee, Jiahua College, responded: It disagreed with the appellant Jiahua Company's appeal claims. Jiahua Company's claim to exercise the right to information against Jiahua College had no legal basis. Jiahua College was governed only by the *Private Education Promotion Law* and its implementing regulations, not by the *Company Law*. Jiahua Company did not have a right to information against Jiahua College. No basis for such a claim could be found in the articles of association of Jiahua College. The articles of association of Jiahua College dated April 9, 2010, had already become invalid. Even if sponsors had the right to "participate in the operation and management activities of the College," it could not lead to the conclusion that sponsors had the right to inspect or reproduce board resolutions, supervisory board resolutions, financial accounting reports, accounting books, etc. For sponsors to exercise the right to information against a private school, there must be explicit provisions of law. The *Private Education Promotion Law* and its implementing regulations contain no such provisions, so sponsors have no right to claim the exercise of the right to information. The first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly. Therefore, Jiahua College requested the appellate court to dismiss the appeal and affirm the original judgment in accordance with the law.

Opinion of the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court at Second Instance:

The issue in dispute at second instance is: whether the appellant Jiahua Company has the right to inspect and reproduce the articles of association, resolutions of the board of directors, resolutions of the supervisory board, and financial accounting reports of the appellee Jiahua College, and to inspect its accounting books. The key to resolving this issue lies in clarifying the following three sub-issues:

First, the specific content of the lawful rights and interests of sponsors of private schools.

The appellant Jiahua Company argued that the right to information is the foundation for sponsors to participate in the operation and management activities of the College; without it, the right to participate in operation and management cannot be exercised at all. As a sponsor, Jiahua Company should be entitled to the corresponding right to information. The appellee Jiahua College argued that Jiahua Company does not have the right to information. Even if sponsors have the right to "participate in the operation and management activities of the College," it cannot lead to the conclusion that sponsors have the right to inspect or reproduce board resolutions, supervisory board resolutions, financial accounting reports, accounting books, etc. The court held that the State protects the lawful rights and interests of sponsors of private schools, and such lawful rights and interests should include the right to information. The reasons are as follows:

First, the lawful civil rights and interests of citizens and legal persons are protected by law, and no organization or individual may infringe upon them. Article 5, Paragraph 2, of the *Law of the People's Republic of China on the Promotion of Privately-Run Schools* provides that the State protects the lawful rights and interests of sponsors, principals, faculty, staff, and educatees of private schools. "Lawful rights and interests" refer to rights and interests that conform to legal provisions. Admittedly, from a literal interpretation alone, it is difficult to determine whether the right to information is included in "lawful rights and interests"; it is necessary to explore this using other methods of legal interpretation.

Second, with respect to the lawful rights and interests of civil subjects, the *Tort Liability Law* enumerates personal and property rights and interests including the right to life, the right to health, the right to name, the right to reputation, the right to honor, the right to portrait, the right to privacy, the right to marital autonomy, the right to guardianship, ownership, usufructuary rights, security interests, copyright, patent rights, trademark rights, the right to discovery, shareholders' rights, and the right of inheritance. The *Company Law* provides that shareholders have various rights, including the right to information. The *Partnership Enterprise Law* also provides that partners have the right to inspect accounting books and other financial materials of the partnership enterprise. All the aforementioned rights fall within the lawful rights and interests that the law seeks to protect. Therefore, from the perspective of the overall legal system, sponsors, as the investors in private schools, should enjoy lawful rights and interests that include the right to know and obtain important information about the school's operation and management activities. This right is an important foundation for sponsors to obtain reasonable returns in accordance with law, participate in major decision-making, and select managers.

Finally, although the *Private Education Promotion Law* does not explicitly provide for such a right, logically speaking, the lawful rights and interests of sponsors, which are not outside the scope of civil rights, should include the right to information. Documents such as the school's articles of association, resolutions of the board of directors, resolutions of the supervisory board, financial accounting reports, and accounting books are important carriers that record and reflect the organization and activities, assets and financial management, and other contents of the school. Only on the basis of obtaining information on the school's operation and management activities can sponsors participate in the school's major decisions and exercise supervision rights. Therefore, the sponsor's right to request inspection and reproduction of the articles of association, resolutions of the board of directors, resolutions of the supervisory board, and financial accounting reports, and to request inspection of the accounting books, are all encompassed within the right to information and should be protected.

Second, the legal basis for sponsors of private schools to enjoy the right to information.

The appellant Jiahua Company argued that the *Private Education Promotion Law* contains no prohibitive provision preventing sponsors from exercising the right to information. The appellee Jiahua College argued that since the *Private Education Promotion Law* and its implementing regulations contain no relevant provisions, sponsors have no right to claim the exercise of the right to information. That sponsors enjoy the right to information is consistent with the value judgment of law. The reasons are as follows:

First, "There are no rights without obligations, and no obligations without rights." Article 8, Paragraph 1, of the *Regulations for the Implementation of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Promotion of Privately-Run Schools* provides: "Sponsors shall perform their obligation to contribute capital on time and in full. During the existence of a private school, sponsors shall not withdraw their capital contributions or misappropriate school funds." While sponsors fulfill their capital contribution obligations and transfer their property ownership, they should enjoy corresponding rights. The right to information is the foundation for sponsors to exercise other rights. Article 51 of the *Law of the People's Republic of China on the Promotion of Privately-Run Schools* provides: "After deducting operating costs, setting aside development funds, and withholding other necessary expenses as prescribed by the State, sponsors may obtain a reasonable return from the surplus of the school. The specific measures for obtaining a reasonable return shall be prescribed by the State Council." Article 44, Paragraph 1, of the *Regulations for the Implementation of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Promotion of Privately-Run Schools* provides: "If sponsors require a reasonable return in accordance with the provisions of the school's articles of association, they may obtain a return at a certain proportion from the school's surplus at the end of each accounting year." Article 25 of the articles of association of Jiahua College also provides: "Sponsors require a reasonable return." The realization of the sponsor's reasonable return as an investor cannot be separated from the protection of the right to information.

Second, sponsors' enjoyment of the right to information helps public schools that participate in establishing private schools to fulfill their duty of supervising State-owned assets. Article 6, Paragraph 2, of the *Regulations for the Implementation of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Promotion of Privately-Run Schools* provides that public schools that participate in establishing private schools shall enjoy the rights and interests of sponsors in accordance with law and shall fulfill the obligation of managing State-owned assets to prevent the loss of State-owned assets. In other words, public schools may also be sponsors of private schools. The rights and interests they enjoy should be no different from those of other sponsors. The right to information is also an important guarantee for public schools to fulfill their duty of supervising State-owned assets.

Finally, sponsors' enjoyment of the right to information is consistent with the legislative purpose of the *Private Education Promotion Law*. Article 3, Paragraph 2, of the General Provisions of the *Law of the People's Republic of China on the Promotion of Privately-Run Schools* provides that the State implements a policy of active encouragement, vigorous support, correct guidance, and lawful management with respect to private education. Article 5, Paragraph 1, provides that the State protects the lawful rights and interests of sponsors, principals, faculty, staff, and educatees of private schools. The General Provisions summarize the general, principled, and abstract content of the legislative ideology, value orientation, and basic principles that run through the entire law. The legislative provisions in the General Provisions of the *Private Education Promotion Law* have a guiding role in interpreting the lawful rights and interests of sponsors of private schools. Therefore, protecting the basic right to information of sponsors, allowing them to understand the education and management activities of private schools and to inspect financial accounting reports or accounting books, is an inherent part of encouraging sponsors to enter the field of private education and promoting the healthy development of private education.

Third, the exercise of the right to information by sponsors of private schools.

The *Private Education Promotion Law* does not directly provide for the exercise of the right to information by sponsors. However, given that the main characteristics of this case are similar to the shareholders' right to information under the *Company Law*, the relevant provisions of the *Company Law* may be applied by analogy. The reasons are as follows:

First, although the sponsor's right to information lacks a legal provision, this does not mean that the sponsor does not enjoy such a right. "Lawful rights and interests" is itself an uncertain concept, which highly summarizes and abstracts social life phenomena, thereby giving it greater inclusiveness. Where there is no provision, it is not a deliberate omission by the legislature. In exploring the intent of the legal norms, the court should actively establish provisions on the right to information to implement the protection of sponsors' lawful rights and interests.

Second, private schools have legal personality, and the relevant provisions of the *Company Law* may be applied by reference. Private schools are legal-person-type private non-enterprise units. Although they are not established for the purpose of profit, this does not mean they do not generate profit. While they differ in their basis and procedures of establishment from companies generally governed by the *Company Law*, there is no difference in the substantive aspects of having legal personality and operating with a profit-making nature. The law provides that sponsors may stipulate in the school's articles of association that they require a reasonable return. Such a return has a property-related characteristic and is directly or indirectly related to property, indicating that sponsors will enjoy property rights and interests after making capital contributions. The *Private Education Promotion Law* distinguishes between for-profit and non-profit private schools, clearly providing that the surplus and remaining property of for-profit private schools shall be distributed in accordance with the provisions of the *Company Law*. Considering comprehensively the business scope, organizational structure, educational level, form of education, and internal management system of Jiahua College, it is not inappropriate to apply, by reference, the relevant provisions of the *Company Law*, which are similar in nature to this case.

Finally, "Similar cases should be treated in the same manner." In judicial practice, the transfer of sponsors' investment shares in private schools applies the *Company Law* by reference; the bankruptcy and liquidation of legal-person-type private non-enterprise units applies the *Enterprise Bankruptcy Law* and other provisions by reference. In this regard, "arguing from the lighter to the heavier," the appellant Jiahua Company, as a sponsor of the appellee Jiahua College, enjoys rights equivalent or similar to those of company shareholders with respect to the right to information. This case may apply the relevant provisions of the *Company Law* by reference to address the exercise of the rights claimed by the sponsor of the private school.

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held that the *Company Law* of China provides that shareholders have the right to inspect and reproduce the company's articles of association, minutes of shareholders' meetings, resolutions of the board of directors, resolutions of the supervisory board, and the company's financial accounting reports. Shareholders may request to inspect the company's accounting books. A shareholder requesting to inspect the company's accounting books shall submit a written request to the company, stating the purpose. If the company has reasonable grounds to believe that the shareholder's request to inspect the accounting books is for an improper purpose and may harm the lawful interests of the company, it may refuse to provide the inspection and shall, within 15 days from the date of the shareholder's written request, give a written reply to the shareholder stating the reasons. In this case, the appellant Jiahua Company, as a sponsor of the appellee Jiahua College, requested to inspect and reproduce the articles of association (including amendments), resolutions of the board of directors, resolutions of the supervisory board, and financial accounting reports (including but not limited to balance sheets, income statements, statements of changes in financial position, statements of financial condition, profit distribution statements, and tax returns) of Jiahua College from its establishment in April 2010 to the present. This request has corresponding legal basis and is supported. As for Jiahua Company's claim to inspect the accounting books (including the general ledger, various subsidiary ledgers, accounts receivable/payable ledgers, cash journals, bank journals, fixed asset card lists, original vouchers, and detailed records of bank statement transactions) from its establishment in April 2010 to the present, given that Jiahua Company submitted a written request to Jiahua College and stated the purpose, the claim to inspect the accounting books has corresponding legal basis and is supported. The defenses of Jiahua College are not adopted.

In conclusion, the appellant Jiahua Company's appeal claims have corresponding factual and legal basis and are supported by the court. The first-instance judgment found the facts clearly but applied the law incorrectly and is corrected in accordance with law. Accordingly, pursuant to Article 5 of the *General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China*, Article 5, Paragraph 2, and Article 51 of the *Law of the People's Republic of China on the Promotion of Privately-Run Schools*, Article 9 of the *Regulations for the Implementation of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Promotion of Privately-Run Schools*, and Item (2) of Article 170, Paragraph 1, of the *Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*, the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered a judgment on July 7, 2016:

1. Reversing Civil Judgment No. (2016) Hu 0120 Min Chu No. 511 of the Fengxian District People's Court of Shanghai;

2. The appellee, Shanghai Jiahua Education Training College, shall, within ten days from the date this judgment takes legal effect, provide the articles of association (including amendments), resolutions of the board of directors, resolutions of the supervisory board, and financial accounting reports (including but not limited to balance sheets, income statements, statements of changes in financial position, statements of financial condition, profit distribution statements, and tax returns) from its establishment in April 2010 to the date this judgment takes legal effect, for the appellant, Shanghai Jiahua Enterprise Development Co., Ltd., to inspect and reproduce;

III. The appellee, Shanghai Jiahua Education Training Institute, shall, within 10 days from the effective date of this judgment, provide its accounting books (including general ledger, subsidiary ledgers, current accounts, cash journal, bank journal, fixed asset card schedule, original vouchers, bank statement transaction details, etc.) from its establishment in April 2010 to the effective date of this judgment for inspection by the appellant, Shanghai Jiahua Enterprise Development Co., Ltd.

This judgment is final.
